sections.title: Concrete model, precise argument, and boundary

passages.title: What must a snapshot remember?
passages.text:
Earlier lessons used Euclid to watch numbers change. Now ask a deeper question: do the visible numbers determine the next action? A parcel robot with three waiting parcels may be about to test the tray or about to move a parcel. These are different states, even though the tray looks identical.

Our state is (n, c, o): n is the nonnegative number waiting, c is CHECK, MOVE, or DONE, and o is the number already delivered. CHECK changes only the control badge. MOVE transfers one parcel and returns to CHECK. DONE changes nothing. Output history belongs in the state if a later observer can distinguish it. Omitting o would lose information about what this machine has already reported.

passages.title: Specify a whole computational method · Prove termination, not just one successful run
passages.text:
Let Q contain all triples just described, not only the triples visited in this example. Let I = {(n,CHECK,0): n ≥ 0} be the allowed initial states. Let Ω contain every triple with badge DONE. Define f on every member of Q: CHECK tests whether n is zero; MOVE with n>0 changes (n,MOVE,o) to (n−1,CHECK,o+1); MOVE with n=0 changes its badge to DONE; DONE is fixed. This otherwise branch matters: f must be total even on a state that ordinary runs never visit.

For input x∈I, define x₀=x and xₖ₊₁=f(xₖ). Termination means that some finite xₖ lies in Ω. It does not mean that a simulation merely exhausted its frame budget.

For every active snapshot use the nonnegative rank R(n,CHECK,o)=2n+1 and R(n,MOVE,o)=2n. Every transition that stays active strictly decreases R. A transition from CHECK with n=0 enters DONE; the otherwise MOVE case also enters DONE. There cannot be infinitely many strict decreases of a nonnegative integer. Thus every allowed input terminates. From (n,CHECK,0), the machine takes exactly 2n+1 transitions to DONE, including the final empty-tray test.

The invariant n+o=N, where N is the original input size, is preserved during these runs. At termination n=0, so o=N. Termination and output correctness are separate conclusions.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}f:Q\to Q,\qquad f(q)=q\ (q\in\Omega)\\{}R_{k+1}<R_k\quad\text{while both states are active}\end{gathered}

passages.title: One run cannot certify every input
passages.text:
Change CHECK so that an odd positive n returns to itself forever. The empty input and every even input might still have a successful run after further changes, but that evidence would not establish an algorithm on all nonnegative inputs. A computational method can contain nonterminating computations; an algorithm must terminate for every input in its declared domain.

The empty input is not an error: it takes one CHECK→DONE transition. Two DONE states with different output histories are both fixed yet observably distinct. The complete-state requirement and the universal quantifier over inputs are the new ideas beyond the earlier Euclidean trace.

passages.title: Put control beside the word
passages.text:
A word alone need not identify a computation. Our snapshot is (σ,j): σ is a finite word over the finite alphabet {a,b}, and j is a rule number. Rule 0 searches left to right for the first adjacent ab. If found, it replaces that occurrence by ba and stays at rule 0. If absent, it leaves the word unchanged and enters terminal rule 1. Rule 1 is fixed.

In aabb, the first ab begins at position 1 when positions start at zero. Replacing it produces abab. Both the word and the control number are part of the new snapshot; they are updated as one mathematical step.

passages.title: Make every primitive instruction effective · Effectiveness does not supply termination
passages.text:
More generally, a rule has a pattern θ, replacement φ, no-match destination a, and match destination b. If σ=uθv and u is the shortest possible prefix, the successor word is uφv and the new control is b. If no occurrence exists, retain σ and branch to a. Every word and rule table is finite. Scanning, comparing symbols, and replacing a finite substring are operations that can be carried out mechanically.

We permit an empty pattern explicitly: its first occurrence is at offset zero, so it inserts the replacement before the word. Without that policy “find a match” would be ambiguous. A terminal control number leaves the complete state unchanged.

For this ab→ba system, count pairs of positions r<s with σᵣ=a and σₛ=b. Swapping one adjacent ab to ba removes exactly that pair; its relations to every other letter are unchanged. The nonnegative pair count therefore decreases by one per successful rewrite. Once no ab remains, one final failed search halts. This proves termination for every finite input word.

Now replace a by aa and return to the same rule. Every step is equally effective, but input a grows forever. Finite instructions, deterministic instructions, and terminating instructions are different properties.

passages.title: Encoding is a promise you must keep
passages.text:
The displayed counterexample uses only the finite instruction a→aa and returns to the same rule. Every word in its run still contains a, so an effective next step is always possible and the terminal branch is never taken. This separates effective encoding from universal termination.

A finite alphabet can encode numbers, lists, and control positions, but a proposed encoding must say which strings are legal and how each primitive operation changes them. Arbitrary real numbers cannot all be represented by finite strings, because there are only countably many such strings. An instruction like “replace the word by the answer to any undecidable question” is not made effective merely by naming it.

Try tracing baab: the first change is baba, not bbaa. Choosing a later match would define a different transition rule even if it eventually produced the same terminal word.

passages.title: Let a new case use several earlier cases
passages.text:
Consider the claim P(n): every integer n≥2 can be written as a product of primes. A prime n is already a product with one factor. A composite n can be split as n=ab with 2≤a,b<n. The proof for n may need both P(a) and P(b), rather than only P(n−1). The dependency picture shows these strictly smaller supports.

For instance, 12 can use 3 and 4, while 4 uses 2 twice. A repeated factor is allowed. The finite picture illustrates the proof pattern; the statement concerns every integer at least 2.

passages.title: State the induction hypothesis at its full strength · The first failure would have nowhere to hide
passages.text:
Strong induction from base b says: if P(b) holds, and for every n>b the truth of all P(k) with b≤k<n implies P(n), then P(n) holds for every n≥b. The hypothesis is not a license to assume the conclusion P(n). In the prime-factorization example b=2. The prime case needs no earlier hypothesis. In the composite case both factors are smaller, so their prime products may be concatenated.

This proves existence of a factorization, not its uniqueness. Uniqueness requires additional number-theoretic reasoning and does not follow from the dependency graph.

Suppose a failure exists, and choose the least integer m≥2 for which P(m) is false. It cannot be prime, because then it supplies its own factorization. If m=ab is composite, both a and b lie between 2 and m−1. By minimality neither can fail. Their factorizations multiply to one for m, contradicting the choice of m.

This least-counterexample proof uses the well-ordering of nonnegative integers: every nonempty set has a least member. Ordinary induction gives the same strength by applying it to the bundled proposition Q(n)=P(2)∧P(3)∧⋯∧P(n).

The accompanying construction uses amounts 8, 9, and 10 as its three bases, then adds a 3-unit piece. It is a second strong-induction witness: a new amount n≥11 can use the already established amount n−3.

passages.title: A missing base can invalidate an attractive recurrence
passages.text:
Suppose a proposed construction reduces n to n−2. One base case generally covers only one parity; the other parity needs its own base or another reduction. For example, every integer n≥8 can be formed from 3-unit and 5-unit pieces: 8=3+5, 9=3+3+3, and 10=5+5 are bases; for n≥11 reduce to n−3≥8 and append a 3-unit piece.

An animation of successful cases up to 50 is not this proof. The arbitrary n argument and the explicit bases explain why no later failure can occur.

passages.title: An exact point need not have a finite decimal name
passages.text:
An integer, a rational number, and a real number describe progressively larger domains. A finite decimal is rational, but a real value such as √2 has no finite decimal expansion. A displayed 1.4142 is an approximation, not a new definition of √2. One exact way to specify a real value is a nested sequence of nonempty closed intervals with rational endpoints whose widths approach zero.

Complex numbers add a second coordinate: z=a+bi, with real a,b and i²=−1. The scene starts with z=2+i. Adding 1+i translates it to 3+2i. Multiplying the original z by 1+i instead gives 1+3i. These are two operations on the same original point, not consecutive updates.

passages.title: Bind algebra to plane geometry · Keep exact arithmetic separate from drawn coordinates
passages.text:
For z=a+bi, |z| means its magnitude: the distance √(a²+b²) from the origin. The bar in z̄ denotes its conjugate a−bi, and arg z names an angle from the positive real axis to a nonzero z. Addition acts coordinate by coordinate. Multiplication combines a scale and a rotation: |zw|=|z||w|, and angles add modulo 2π. Here |1+i|=√2 and its angle is π/4, so multiplying by 1+i rotates 45 degrees and stretches by √2. Conjugation changes a+bi into a−bi, reflecting across the real axis; z times its conjugate is a²+b².

The square root in |z|=√(a²+b²) means the nonnegative real square root. In particular, a complex number can have nonzero magnitude without being positive or negative; the usual ordering on real numbers does not extend to an ordered field structure on the complex plane.

The integer-coordinate scene computes addition and multiplication exactly; its pixel coordinates are only a representation. An angle label such as 45° is exact here, while a decimal magnitude such as 1.414214 is rounded. A finite set of plotted points cannot prove identities for all complex numbers.

The multiplication formula follows by distributing four terms and replacing i² by −1. Expanding (ac−bd)²+(ad+bc)² proves |zw|²=(a²+b²)(c²+d²); taking nonnegative square roots proves the magnitude rule. This proof applies to every real a,b,c,d, including zero.

passages.title: Powers need a declared domain
passages.text:
For a positive real base b, define bˣ=exp(x ln b) for real x. The ordinary exponent laws then hold, and logarithms base b require b≠1. Integer powers of a complex number are unambiguous; negative integer powers require a nonzero base. Fractional complex powers require a branch choice or a set of possible values.

Here arg z is an angle of the nonzero point z in the complex plane. Every complex logarithm of a nonzero z has the form ln|z|+i(arg z+2πk), where k is any integer. The principal value chooses one angle interval. Once a branch is chosen, a familiar law may fail literally: principal Log(−1)+Log(−1)=2πi, whereas principal Log(1)=0.

passages.title: Each square owns one pair of indices
passages.text:
A finite double sum is best understood as a collection of labeled terms. In the triangular scene, cell (i,j) exists exactly when 1≤j≤i≤n, and carries value i+j. Summing row by row fixes i and visits j=1,…,i. Summing column by column fixes j and visits i=j,…,n. The cells do not move into a different mathematical set; only the grouping changes.

For a rectangular set of indices, multiplying two sums distributes into every pair: each aᵢ from the first sum meets each bⱼ from the second. Missing a cell would omit a product; counting it twice would change the result.

passages.title: Change bounds when changing the outer index · Prove a rearrangement by matching terms
passages.text:
The precise triangular identity is Σᵢ₌₁ⁿΣⱼ₌₁ⁱ aᵢⱼ = Σⱼ₌₁ⁿΣᵢ₌ⱼⁿ aᵢⱼ. The outer variable is a fixed parameter during the inner sum. A symbol used as a summation index is bound only inside that summation; renaming it is harmless if every occurrence and bound is renamed consistently.

For n=0 the index set is empty and both totals are zero. For n=1 both descriptions contain the single pair (1,1). The reason the formula survives these boundaries is that it describes the same index set, not that we patched the endpoints afterward.

Finite addition is associative and commutative, so any bijection of the finite index set preserves the sum. A proof therefore has two parts: every old pair occurs in the new description, and every new pair was legal before. In a change of variable k=n−j, reverse the endpoints as well as the summand; an increasing old index becomes a decreasing new index.

The rectangular distributive law follows by expanding one factor at a time. The triangular interchange follows from the two equivalent inequalities above. Neither proof depends on the example values i+j; they work for any real or complex aᵢⱼ.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}\{(i,j):1\le j\le i\le n\}=\{(i,j):1\le j\le n,\ j\le i\le n\}\\{}\sum_{j=0}^{n}a_j=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_{n-k}\end{gathered}

passages.title: Infinite sums require another theorem
passages.text:
Finiteness is doing real work. For infinite families, convergence of one ordering alone does not authorize arbitrary rearrangement or interchange. Absolute convergence supplies a safe hypothesis for the usual rearrangement theorem. Later lessons separate that analytic issue from this finite algebra.

A common mistake is to swap the two summation signs while leaving the inner bound i untouched. That can make an index refer to itself or introduce cells above the diagonal. Before simplifying algebra, sketch the legal cells and check a corner such as (1,n).

passages.title: A yes-or-no statement can be a counting weight
passages.text:
For a proposition P whose truth is defined, write [P]=1 when P is true and [P]=0 when P is false. In the scene, A means “the label is even” and B means “the label is divisible by 3.” Adding [A] over labels counts A. Multiplying a defined number by [A] keeps it exactly when A is true.

The overlapping boxes are not merely categories: an object in both boxes receives two copies when [A]+[B] is used. Subtracting [A and B] removes the extra copy. Objects in neither box receive zero throughout.

passages.title: Verify an identity on all truth possibilities · Count exact cases instead of hoping overlap disappears
passages.text:
The formula [A or B]=[A]+[B]−[A and B] is a pointwise identity. For truth pairs (false,false), (true,false), (false,true), and (true,true), the right side is respectively 0,1,1,1. Summing over a finite universe gives inclusion–exclusion for two sets. Also [A and B]=[A][B], and [not A]=1−[A].

For finite U and a real-valued function w defined on U, Σₓ∈U w(x)[P(x)] equals the sum of w over the elements satisfying P. This is weighted filtering, not only counting.

Exactly one of A,B is true when [A]+[B]−2[A and B]=1. This differs from “at least one.” For three conditions, an object satisfying all three is counted three times by the individual counts, subtracted three times by pairwise intersections, and then added once by the triple intersection. Checking the weight of one object proves the general counting rule.

For labels 1 through 10, the even labels number 5, multiples of 3 number 3, and their intersection has only 6. Thus at least one condition holds for 7 labels, whereas exactly one holds for 6.

passages.title: A bracket does not repair an undefined expression
passages.text:
The tempting term [x≠0]/x is still undefined at x=0 in ordinary arithmetic: its denominator is zero before any simplification. Likewise, 0 times an undefined value is not automatically zero. Define a piecewise function instead, or restrict the summation domain to x≠0 before dividing.

This distinction is useful in code too. A short-circuit conditional that avoids evaluating an invalid expression has semantics different from blindly multiplying its value by a boolean. The mathematical specification should make the safe branch explicit.

passages.title: Move equal pieces into alignment
passages.text:
A telescoping sum hides equal positive and negative terms at neighboring indices. For k≥1, 1/[k(k+1)]=1/k−1/(k+1). Put positive terms in one row and negative terms in another. Shift the second row by one position so equal denominators align. Every interior reciprocal cancels, leaving 1−1/(n+1).

The shift is a change of indexing, not a change of value. A minus sign belongs to the entire term. In particular, the final negative term has no partner, and dropping it would give the wrong sum.

passages.title: Weights leave a correction: summation by parts
passages.text:
The forward differences are Δbₖ=bₖ₊₁−bₖ and Δaₖ=aₖ₊₁−aₖ: each is the next value minus the current one. Expand aₖ₊₁bₖ₊₁−aₖbₖ as aₖ(bₖ₊₁−bₖ)+bₖ₊₁(aₖ₊₁−aₖ). Summing this identity telescopes the left side. Moving the second sum to the other side gives a discrete analogue of integration by parts. It is valid for any finite real or complex sequences with all indicated indices defined.

The shifted bₖ₊₁ in the correction is essential. With aₖ=k and bₖ=k, the left side is Σₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ k=n(n−1)/2; the endpoint expression n²−Σₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(k+1) gives the same value.

passages.title: Expose the endpoint formula before substituting values · Use the proof to choose what to telescope
passages.text:
For any sequence b₀,b₁,…,bₙ, the difference sum Σₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹(bₖ₊₁−bₖ)=bₙ−b₀. For n=0 it is an empty sum, hence zero, and both endpoints coincide. For one term it is simply b₁−b₀. These checks prevent off-by-one formulas.

To obtain the reciprocal example, choose bₖ=−1/(k+1). Then bₖ₊₁−bₖ=1/[(k+1)(k+2)] and shift the summation index. Alternatively use positive reciprocals and reverse the sign of the difference.

When a term contains a difference, first ask which neighboring values created it. When it contains a weight times a difference, try summation by parts so that the new difference of the weight is simpler. Constant weights disappear from the correction; linear weights become constants.

No convergence assumption is needed for these finite identities. Passing to an infinite endpoint requires a separate limit argument. The diagram proves neither that every sum telescopes nor that an infinite terminal term can be silently discarded.

passages.title: A product visits factors, not terms to add
passages.text:
The notation ∏ₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖ means multiply the n listed factors. It obeys a recursion P₀=1 and Pₙ=Pₙ₋₁aₙ. The empty product is 1 because multiplying by it must leave another product unchanged. By contrast, the empty sum is 0.

In the scene, factor k is (k+1)/k. The numerator of one factor matches the denominator of the next, so all interior factors cancel. For n≥1 the answer is n+1. For n=0 the product is empty and the same formula gives 1.

passages.title: Cancellation has a nonzero contract · Separate laws that look alike
passages.text:
More generally, if b₀,…,bₙ are all nonzero, then ∏ₖ₌₁ⁿ(bₖ/bₖ₋₁)=bₙ/b₀. Each denominator cancels a matching numerator. The formula can sometimes be extended after algebraic simplification, but the original quotient expression is undefined when a denominator vanishes.

A zero factor makes a defined product zero. An even number of negative factors gives a positive product; an odd number gives a negative product. Neither observation changes the empty-product convention.

For finite scalar products, ∏(aₖbₖ)=(∏aₖ)(∏bₖ), because multiplication is associative and commutative. But ∏(aₖ+bₖ) is generally not ∏aₖ+∏bₖ. Expanding the product requires one choice from every pair and includes all mixed choices. In the formula, S is the subset of positions where we choose aₖ; positions outside S choose bₖ. The sum over S visits every such subset once. Already (a+b)(c+d)=ac+ad+bc+bd.

A product of matrices cannot be freely reordered, even though parentheses can be changed. State the domain before importing a scalar identity into another algebraic setting.

passages.title: Count the factors before you simplify
passages.text:
The boundary scene separates three cases: no factors gives 1; a defined zero factor gives 0; a zero denominator is undefined. These are different mathematical situations even if a programming language displays a similar empty or zero value.

The integer interval m≤k≤n contains n−m+1 indices when m≤n, and none when m>n. Thus a constant product over m≤k≤n equals c to that number of factors; the empty case uses c⁰=1 by the product convention, including when c=0 in this combinatorial setting. This convention should not be confused with an indeterminate analytic limit.

Taking logarithms is safe for positive real factors and converts products to sums. With negative or complex factors, branch choices prevent an unrestricted logarithm law. A direct product proof avoids that issue.

passages.title: An infinite sum is a limit of finite sums
passages.text:
For a real sequence a₁,a₂,…, define the partial sum Sₙ=Σₖ₌₁ⁿaₖ. The infinite series has value S when, for every ε>0, some N makes |Sₙ−S|<ε for all n≥N. The picture shows finite partial sums of 1/2+1/4+1/8+⋯. After n terms the unfilled length is exactly 2⁻ⁿ.

This is more than a pleasing plot: given ε, choose N with 2⁻ᴺ<ε. Every later gap is smaller. A controlled tail converts the finite calculation into a proof of convergence.

passages.title: Absolute convergence protects rearrangements · A stopping rule needs a bound, not a flat-looking curve
passages.text:
A series is absolutely convergent if Σ|aₖ| converges. It is conditionally convergent if Σaₖ converges but Σ|aₖ| does not. For example, the alternating harmonic series converges: consecutive pairs are positive, the even partial sums increase, the odd partial sums decrease, and their gap tends to zero. Its tail after n terms has magnitude at most 1/(n+1). Its absolute-value series is harmonic and diverges.

Absolute convergence permits arbitrary permutations without changing the sum. Conditional convergence does not: taking positive terms until a target is exceeded, then negative terms until it is crossed downward, can produce a different limit.

To approximate a convergent sum within 1/1000, choose a truncation from a proven tail estimate. For the picture’s geometric sum, n=10 suffices because 2⁻¹⁰=1/1024<1/1000. Merely observing that consecutive screen values round to the same decimal says little about the remaining tail.

The displayed model is exact for its finite rational sums. It does not claim to compute infinitely many additions or to prove convergence from a finite number of trials. The epsilon argument, not the animation, is the proof.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}\sum |a_k|<\infty\Rightarrow\text{every rearrangement has the same sum}\\{}\text{displayed finite data}+\text{proved tail bound}\Rightarrow\text{certified accuracy}\end{gathered}

passages.title: A term approaching zero is necessary, not sufficient
passages.text:
If Sₙ converges, then aₙ=Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁ approaches zero. The converse is false. The harmonic terms 1/n approach zero, but grouping indices 2ʲ<k≤2ʲ⁺¹ gives 2ʲ terms each at least 1/2ʲ⁺¹. Each group adds at least 1/2, so the partial sums exceed every fixed bound.

For a geometric series Σₖ₌₀∞rᵏ, the finite identity Sₙ=(1−rⁿ⁺¹)/(1−r) leads to convergence only when |r|<1. At r=1 the sums grow; at r=−1 they oscillate. A finite formula does not itself authorize a limit.

passages.title: Find the two neighboring integer fences
passages.text:
For a real x, floor(x) is the greatest integer not exceeding x, and ceiling(x) is the least integer not smaller than x. On a number line, floor is the fence at or to the left; ceiling is the fence at or to the right. At an integer the two fences coincide.

For −7/3, the floor is −3 and the ceiling is −2. Truncation toward zero would give −2, so it is not floor. The fractional part {x}=x−floor(x) is 2/3, a nonnegative distance from the left fence, even though x is negative.

passages.title: Use integer quantifiers to turn pictures into implications · Translate and reflect the integer grid
passages.text:
For any integer m, floor(x)≥m if and only if x≥m. Also floor(x)<m if and only if x<m. These follow from the interval containing x and the fact that no integer lies strictly between consecutive integers. For ceiling, ceiling(x)≤m if and only if x≤m, and ceiling(x)>m if and only if x>m.

The qualification “m is an integer” is essential. For x=1.8 and m=1.5, x≥m is true while floor(x)≥m is false. Inequalities must not lose that domain condition.

Adding an integer m translates all fences, so floor(x+m)=floor(x)+m. Reflecting the line reverses order, giving floor(−x)=−ceiling(x). If x is not an integer, ceiling(x)=floor(x)+1; at an integer they are equal instead.

Write x=a+u and y=b+v, where a,b are integers and 0≤u,v<1. Then floor(x+y)=a+b+floor(u+v). The final floor is either 0 or 1: the extra unit is a carry created by the fractional parts. This proves a useful bound without guessing from examples.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}m\in\mathbb Z:\quad\lfloor x\rfloor<m\iff x<m\\{}\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor\le\lfloor x+y\rfloor\le\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor y\rfloor+1\end{gathered}

passages.title: Equality at a fence changes the answer
passages.text:
A floor interval includes its left endpoint and excludes its right endpoint. A ceiling interval does the reverse. Replacing a strict inequality by a non-strict one at an endpoint can add an entire unwanted integer case. Test x=0, a negative integer, and values just to either side of an integer.

For n≥0 objects packed at most d per box with positive integer d, the minimum box count is ceiling(n/d). It is zero for n=0. The equivalent expression floor((n−1)/d)+1 also works at n=0: floor(−1/d)=−1. Replacing floor by truncation toward zero would break that empty-input case when d>1.

passages.title: A remainder is a representative; congruence is a relation
passages.text:
For integer a and positive integer m, define a mod m = a−m floor(a/m). It is the unique remainder r with 0≤r<m for which a=qm+r with integer q. For example, −8=−2·5+2, so −8 mod 5=2. A programming language that truncates division toward zero may return a different signed remainder.

The relation a≡b (mod m) means that m divides a−b. It is equivalent to the equality of their chosen remainders, but it is a statement about a pair of numbers, not a number-valued operation.

passages.title: Multiplication maps residue classes to residue classes · Cancellation needs the right modulus
passages.text:
If a≡b and c≡d modulo m, then a+c≡b+d and ac≡bd. The proof writes a=b+um and c=d+vm and expands; every difference is a multiple of m. Thus modular arithmetic can reduce intermediate sums and products without changing the final residue.

The scene multiplies every residue by a fixed multiplier. It is a permutation exactly when that multiplier is relatively prime to m. When gcd(a,m)=1, Bézout gives integers u,v with ua+vm=1, so u is a multiplicative inverse of a modulo m.

From ax≡ay modulo m, division by a is valid modulo m only when gcd(a,m)=1. In general let d=gcd(a,m); then m divides a(x−y) exactly when m/d divides x−y. The valid reduced conclusion is x≡y modulo m/d.

For 2x≡2y modulo 6, x=1 and y=4 are a counterexample to cancellation modulo 6: both products have remainder 2, yet the original residues differ. They do agree modulo 3, as the general rule predicts.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}\gcd(a,m)=1\Rightarrow\exists u:\ ua\equiv1\pmod m\\{}ax\equiv ay\pmod m\iff x\equiv y\pmod{m/\gcd(a,m)}\end{gathered}

passages.title: The source’s real remainder extension has different bounds
passages.text:
The source also defines x mod y=x−y floor(x/y) for real x and nonzero real y. When y>0 the result lies in [0,y); when y<0 it lies in (y,0]. Its separate convention at y=0 is x mod 0=x. The runtime here uses positive integer moduli only; the real extension should not be confused with integer divisibility.

Modulo 1, every integer remainder is zero and all integers are congruent. Modular inverses in the usual nontrivial residue system are discussed for m≥2. Never infer that dividing a congruence is harmless because adding and multiplying are harmless.

passages.title: A prime prevents nonzero collisions
passages.text:
Let p be prime and let a be an integer not divisible by p. If ax≡ay modulo p, then p divides a(x−y). Because p does not divide a, it divides x−y. Thus multiplying the nonzero residues 1,…,p−1 by a is injective, hence a permutation of this finite set.

The picture includes residue 0 so the whole map is visible; 0 stays 0 and the remaining tiles rearrange. The theorem below uses the product of only the nonzero residues, because including zero would destroy the cancellable product.

passages.title: Cancel the product to obtain Fermat’s theorem · Combine coprime moduli by an explicit construction
passages.text:
Multiply every nonzero residue before and after the permutation. This gives aᵖ⁻¹(p−1)!≡(p−1)! modulo p. None of the factors in (p−1)! is divisible by p, so the product is invertible and may be canceled. Therefore aᵖ⁻¹≡1 when p does not divide a.

Multiplying by a gives aᵖ≡a. The latter formula is true even when p divides a, because then both sides are zero modulo p. Do not apply the exponent p−1 version to multiples of p.

Let r,s≥2 be coprime integers and suppose x≡u modulo r and x≡v modulo s. Set x=u+rt. Since r has an inverse r⁻¹ modulo s, choose t≡(v−u)r⁻¹ modulo s. This constructs a solution. If x and y satisfy both conditions, r and s divide x−y; coprimality makes rs divide x−y. Thus the solution is unique modulo rs.

For x≡2 modulo 5 and x≡1 modulo 3, write x=2+5t. Then 2t≡2 modulo 3, so t≡1 and x≡7 modulo 15.
passages.formula: \begin{gathered}p\nmid a\Rightarrow a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,\qquad a^p\equiv a\pmod p\\{}x=u+r\bigl((v-u)r^{-1}\bmod s\bigr)\pmod{rs}\end{gathered}

passages.title: Do not turn the theorem into a false primality test
passages.text:
A composite modulus may satisfy a Fermat congruence for some bases. For example, 2³⁴⁰≡1 modulo 341 although 341=11·31. Checking one base is therefore not a proof of primality. When a shares a factor with the modulus, multiplication can have collisions, and the permutation proof fails.

For noncoprime r,s, simultaneous congruences are compatible only when u≡v modulo gcd(r,s), and a compatible solution is unique modulo lcm(r,s), not necessarily rs. For instance, x≡0 modulo 4 and x≡1 modulo 6 have no solution because their parity requirements conflict.

passages.title: An ordered choice uses a shrinking supply
passages.text:
Five distinct badges can fill three ordered positions in 5·4·3 ways. There are five choices for the first slot, four remaining choices for the second, and three for the third. The scene displays one particular prefix, but the count beside it counts all possible prefixes of that length. Do not confuse one displayed arrangement with the whole collection.

For n distinct objects and 0≤k≤n ordered slots without replacement, the count is n(n−1)⋯(n−k+1)=n!/(n−k)!. It is also called a falling factorial.

passages.title: Repeated labels require a quotient argument · Identify what the observer can distinguish
passages.text:
Suppose n badges carry repeated labels with multiplicities m₁,…,mᵣ summing to n. Temporarily label every badge individually. There are n! labeled arrangements. For any fixed visible word, rearranging the identities within each repeated label produces exactly m₁!⋯mᵣ! labeled arrangements. Every visible word has the same number of preimages, so division gives n!/(m₁!⋯mᵣ!).

For the multiset A,A,B,B,C, this yields 5!/(2!2!1!)=30 visible words. Simply applying the distinct-object formula would overcount.

A lineup, a subset, and a necklace have different equivalences. A subset forgets all k! orders of its chosen members. A circular seating may identify rotations, but reflections need not be equivalent; repeated labels can also change orbit sizes. Never divide by a symmetry count without checking that every outcome is overcounted equally.

Our model checks distinct-object counts against explicit enumeration for n≤7. That verifies the implementation on small cases. The arbitrary-length multiplication and equal-fiber arguments prove the formulas for all allowed n.

passages.title: Factorial is the full-length special case
passages.text:
When k=n, every object is placed and the count is n!. Define 0!=1: there is exactly one ordering of no objects, the empty ordering. Likewise P(n,0)=1, since making no choices is one possible result. If k>n, no injective arrangement exists and its counting value is zero; the factorial quotient should not be evaluated at a negative factorial.

The multiplication rule counts a decision tree when every prefix at the same depth has the same number of possible next choices. With constraints that change that number, summing branch counts may be necessary.

passages.title: A factorial contains layers of prime factors
passages.text:
The symbol νₚ(n!) means the number of copies of prime p in the prime factorization of n!. To count those copies, count how many factors contribute at least one p, how many contribute an additional p, and so on. Multiples of p contribute the first layer, multiples of p² the second, and multiples of p³ the third. Thus the exponent is the sum of floor(n/pʲ) for j≥1. Only finitely many terms are nonzero.

For 10! and p=2 the layers contribute 5+2+1=8. The factor 8 is correctly counted three times, because 8 contains three copies of 2. Each colored block in the scene represents one copy, not one whole integer factor.

passages.title: Compare exact growth with a controlled preview · Large integers and logarithms answer different questions
passages.text:
Here e≈2.71828 is the base of natural logarithms, and exp(x)=eˣ is the natural exponential function. Stirling’s leading estimate is Lₙ=√(2πn)(n/e)ⁿ for positive integer n. Its asymptotic meaning is n!/Lₙ→1, not that their difference tends to zero. A useful quantitative form is Lₙ exp(1/(12n+1))<n!<Lₙ exp(1/(12n)). We use this classical bound as a stated result here; its analytic proof belongs to the later asymptotic-analysis material.

Compute relative error as |Lₙ−n!|/n!, rather than only absolute error. An estimate can have a small relative error while missing by an enormous integer amount.

Exact factorials use integer arithmetic. A decimal digit count can be estimated from log₁₀(n!)=Σₖ₌₁ⁿlog₁₀k, but a floating estimate near an integer boundary needs an error bound before flooring. Logarithms help compare scales without overflowing; they do not reproduce every digit.

Trailing decimal zeros equal min(ν₂(n!),ν₅(n!)); in a factorial the 5-count is the smaller one. At n=0 the factorial is 1 and all prime valuations are zero. Stirling’s displayed expression is reserved for n≥1.

passages.title: Prove the layer count by interchanging finite sums
passages.text:
Let νₚ(k) be the largest e≥0 with pᵉ dividing k, for positive integer k and prime p. Then νₚ(n!)=Σₖ₌₁ⁿνₚ(k). Express νₚ(k) as Σⱼ≥₁[pʲ divides k], and interchange the finite nonzero terms. The inner count of multiples of pʲ is floor(n/pʲ).

Primality matters because prime exponents add in products. For a composite “base” such as 4, separate factors 2 and 2 can combine into a factor 4; counting only multiples of powers of 4 misses such contributions. The displayed valuation function is deliberately defined for prime p.

passages.title: A smooth extension needs more than a lookup table
passages.text:
Factorials prescribe values at nonnegative integers, but infinitely many functions agree there. The gamma function is a principled extension: for real x>0, Γ(x)=∫₀∞tˣ⁻¹e⁻ᵗ dt. This positive improper integral converges. Near zero, tˣ⁻¹ is integrable exactly for x>0; at infinity the exponential dominates every fixed power.

The scene uses x=1, where the curve is simply e⁻ᵗ. It brackets the area on [0,T] by left and right rectangles, then adds the exact tail e⁻ᵀ. The printed decimal endpoints are rounded approximations to analytical bounds. The inequality between the exact rectangle sums and the integral follows from monotonicity.

passages.title: Integration by parts recovers the recurrence
passages.text:
For x>0, integration by parts gives Γ(x+1)=xΓ(x). The endpoint tˣe⁻ᵗ vanishes both at zero and infinity, so there is no leftover boundary term. Also Γ(1)=∫₀∞e⁻ᵗdt=1. Induction then yields Γ(n+1)=n! for every nonnegative integer n.

The half-integer value Γ(1/2)=√π follows by substituting t=u² and using the Gaussian integral. That Gaussian integral is a separate theorem, not established by our one-dimensional rectangle display. The recurrence therefore gives Γ(3/2)=√π/2 and Γ(5/2)=3√π/4.

passages.title: The recurrence alone does not select gamma · Continuation and numerical accuracy have boundaries
passages.text:
If h(x) is any nonconstant positive function of period 1 with h(1)=1, then G(x)=h(x)Γ(x) also satisfies G(x+1)=xG(x) and agrees with factorial values at positive integers. For example, h(x)=exp(c sin(2πx)) with nonzero real c has these properties. Thus interpolation and recurrence do not imply uniqueness.

A classical characterization adds positivity and logarithmic convexity on x>0, together with G(1)=1; these select Γ. We state this characterization to explain what extra structure is needed, without pretending to prove the characterization here.

The source also gives Euler’s limit Γ(x)=lim as m→∞ of mˣm!/[x(x+1)⋯(x+m)], initially for x>0. The integral route here is an equivalent standard construction; the equivalence is not proved by the rectangle animation.

The recurrence extends Γ to negative noninteger real arguments, and complex analysis gives a meromorphic continuation to the complex plane. It has poles at 0,−1,−2,…, so writing Γ(0) as an ordinary finite value is invalid. Two advanced source formulas deserve precise statements. Reflection: Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=π/sin(πz) for complex z not an integer. Hankel: 1/Γ(z)=(1/(2πi))∫_H eᵗt⁻ᶻdt, valid for every complex z, with the reciprocal gamma extended as an entire function. The contour H comes from −∞ below the negative real axis, circles the origin counterclockwise at a fixed positive radius, then returns above the negative axis. Use t⁻ᶻ=exp(−z Log t), with −π<arg(t)<π and the corresponding limiting values on the two rays. A radius-to-zero limit is not being asserted for arbitrary z. These are stated complex-analysis theorems; proving them requires analytic continuation, contour integration, and branch conventions beyond this unit. At a gamma pole, reciprocal gamma is zero rather than an undefined ordinary quotient.

For the displayed x=1 integral, decreasing e⁻ᵗ gives rigorous finite rectangle bounds. Increasing the rectangle count tightens their difference; increasing T controls the omitted tail. A generic numerical quadrature output without a proven bound would not certify an arbitrary gamma value.

passages.title: Connect the source’s Euler limit to the integral
passages.text:
The source’s Euler limit is another exact definition, not a polynomial interpolation through integer factorials. For real x>0, define L_N(x)=N! Nˣ/[x(x+1)⋯(x+N)], where N is a positive integer. The claim is Γ(x)=lim as N→∞ of L_N(x). Our scene computes these finite ratios with exact rational arithmetic for x=2. Cancelling N! leaves N²/[(N+1)(N+2)]; the inner square and outer rectangle show why the ratio is below 1 and approaches it. The smaller help uses x=1 and the ratio N/(N+1).

Advanced bridge to the integral definition: repeated integration by parts, with the base integral ∫₀¹uˣ⁻¹du=1/x, gives ∫₀¹uˣ⁻¹(1−u)ᴺdu=N!/[x(x+1)⋯(x+N)]. Multiply by Nˣ and substitute t=Nu to get L_N(x)=∫₀ᴺtˣ⁻¹(1−t/N)ᴺdt. Extend the integrand by zero beyond N. For each fixed t>0 it tends to tˣ⁻¹e⁻ᵗ, and 0≤(1−t/N)ᴺ≤e⁻ᵗ on 0≤t≤N. The dominating function tˣ⁻¹e⁻ᵗ is integrable for x>0. The dominated convergence theorem therefore proves the limit equals Γ(x).

This bridge uses improper integration, integration by parts, and dominated convergence as prerequisites. It does not infer an infinite limit from the three displayed ratios. For nonpositive noninteger arguments, continuation is handled separately; direct substitutions at poles are excluded.

passages.title: Three rows, three meanings of a power
passages.text:
An ordinary power xᵏ multiplies k copies of x. A falling factorial x underlined k multiplies x,x−1,…,x−k+1. A rising factorial x overlined k multiplies x,x+1,…,x+k−1. Here k is a nonnegative integer and x may be real or complex. Every empty product at k=0 is 1.

For x=5 and k=3, the three values are 125,60,210. The rows make the difference visible: position j changes the factor only in the falling and rising rows. A notation that hides this shift can encourage invalid ordinary exponent laws.

passages.title: Split a factorial power with a shifted base · Discrete differences lower the degree cleanly
passages.text:
Split the product for x underlined (m+n) after the first m factors. The remaining factors start at x−m, so x underlined (m+n) equals (x underlined m)((x−m) underlined n). For rising powers, the second base is x+m. These formulas hold for nonnegative integer m,n and every real or complex x because they are product identities.

They are not the ordinary exponent law with the same base in both factors. For instance, 5 underlined 2 times 5 underlined 1 is 100, but 5 underlined 3 is 60.

Let Δf(x)=f(x+1)−f(x). Factoring the common k−1 factors in (x+1) underlined k minus x underlined k gives Δ(x underlined k)=k x underlined (k−1) for k≥1. This is why factorial powers are natural for discrete summation.

Summing from x=0 through n−1 yields Σₓ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ x underlined k = n underlined (k+1)/(k+1) for k≥0. The starting endpoint 0 underlined (k+1) vanishes. The formula includes k=0: summing n copies of 1 gives n.

passages.title: Reverse the factors or negate each one
passages.text:
Reversing the order of a rising product gives x overlined k=(x+k−1) underlined k. Extracting a minus sign from every factor gives x overlined k=(−1)ᵏ(−x) underlined k. These are polynomial identities and remain meaningful even when a factor is zero.

For positive x where the gamma quotients are finite, x overlined k=Γ(x+k)/Γ(x). Similarly x underlined k=Γ(x+1)/Γ(x−k+1) where that quotient is defined. At a gamma pole, use the product polynomial or an explicitly justified continuation, rather than dividing undefined values.

sections.title: Concrete model, precise argument, and boundary

passages.title: Forget the order, but keep the members
passages.text:
For nonnegative integer n and integer k with 0≤k≤n, the binomial coefficient counts k-element subsets of n distinct objects. Each subset has k! ordered listings. The n underlined k injective listings therefore divide into equal groups of k!, giving n!/[k!(n−k)!].

Choosing the omitted objects instead gives a bijection between k-subsets and (n−k)-subsets, which proves symmetry. The empty subset is unique, so choosing zero objects gives 1. If k<0 or k>n, no such subset exists and the counting value is 0.

passages.title: Build Pascal’s triangle by a disjoint decision · A diagonal sum can be partitioned by the largest member
passages.text:
Mark one of the n objects. A k-subset either excludes it, leaving a k-subset of the other n−1 objects, or includes it, leaving a (k−1)-subset of those objects. The two cases do not overlap and cover every subset. Their counts add.

The scene draws an edge from each contributing parent to its child. Missing parents outside the triangle have count zero. Row zero begins with one empty subset. The sum of row n is 2ⁿ because each of the n objects can independently be included or excluded.

For fixed integer m≥0, Σₖ₌₀ⁿ C(k,m)=C(n+1,m+1). Count (m+1)-subsets of {1,…,n+1} by their largest member k+1, where 0≤k≤n. The other m members must come from {1,…,k}, giving C(k,m) possibilities for this case.

This “hockey-stick” identity follows by repeated Pascal addition too. Terms with k<m vanish automatically. A precise convention for out-of-range lower indices makes the boundary cases painless.

passages.title: The algebraic extension has a different domain
passages.text:
For any real or complex r and nonnegative integer k, define C(r,k)=r underlined k/k!. This polynomial definition agrees with subset counts when r=n is a nonnegative integer, but a noninteger upper index no longer literally counts subsets. Define C(r,k)=0 for negative integer k.

Pascal’s identity extends to all r by polynomial algebra for each fixed nonnegative k. Symmetry C(r,k)=C(r,r−k) does not transfer unqualified: r−k may not even be an integer lower index. Keep counting arguments in their declared integer domain.

passages.title: Every factor contributes one choice
passages.text:
Expand (a+b)ⁿ with n a nonnegative integer. A term in the full distributive expansion is specified by a word of n choices, each a or b. If exactly k positions choose b, the term becomes aⁿ⁻ᵏbᵏ. There are C(n,k) such position sets, so equal monomials combine into the finite binomial theorem.

The scene preserves each choice word while regrouping it by its number of b’s. Coefficients arise from how many words land in a group; they are not additional choices made after the expansion.

passages.title: Substitution produces useful sum identities · A noninteger exponent gives an infinite expansion
passages.text:
Set a=b=1 to obtain Σₖ C(n,k)=2ⁿ. Set a=1,b=−1 to obtain Σₖ(−1)ᵏC(n,k)=0 for n≥1. For n=0, both sums are 1 because the expansion contains its one empty product. Differentiating the finite polynomial (1+z)ⁿ gives Σₖ kC(n,k)zᵏ⁻¹=n(1+z)ⁿ⁻¹. At z=1 this yields Σₖ kC(n,k)=n2ⁿ⁻¹ for n≥1.

These manipulations are finite polynomial operations, so no infinite-series convergence issue arises.

For real r and real z with |z|<1, the generalized binomial theorem says (1+z)ʳ=Σₖ≥₀ C(r,k)zᵏ, using the falling-product definition of C(r,k). The ratio of successive nonzero term magnitudes approaches |z|, giving absolute convergence inside this interval. The coefficient recurrence (k+1)cₖ₊₁=(r−k)cₖ makes the resulting series satisfy (1+z)F′=rF with F(0)=1; uniqueness of this differential equation identifies F=(1+z)ʳ.

For r=−1 the coefficients alternate signs and the formula is the geometric series for 1/(1+z). This is the model’s separately controlled generalized example.

passages.title: Boundary points require their own analysis
passages.text:
Do not substitute z=1 or z=−1 merely because a plot looks smooth inside the convergence interval. For r=−1 and z=1, the partial sums 1−1+1−1+⋯ oscillate even though 1/(1+1)=1/2 exists. At z=−1 the function itself has a pole and the series terms are all 1.

For a nonnegative integer exponent, the series terminates and the finite theorem is valid for every real or complex z. The domain changes because there are only finitely many nonzero coefficients, not because endpoint convergence was silently assumed.

passages.title: Start from factors when the upper index is negative
passages.text:
For integer k≥0 and real r, C(r,k)=r(r−1)⋯(r−k+1)/k!. Replacing r by −r gives k negative factors. Extracting each minus sign leaves r(r+1)⋯(r+k−1), which is the reversed falling product for upper index r+k−1. Thus C(−r,k)=(−1)ᵏC(r+k−1,k).

For example C(−4,3)=−20. It is perfectly defined by a polynomial product even though (−4)! is not an ordinary factorial. The diagram tracks the sign separately from the positive factors.

passages.title: Prefer a division-free identity when a denominator may vanish · Choose in stages and then change which stage comes first
passages.text:
For k≥1, canceling a common product gives kC(r,k)=rC(r−1,k−1). Dividing by k is safe in this domain. Another absorption relation is (r−k)C(r,k)=rC(r−1,k). This division-free form is valid for all real r and fixed nonnegative integer k. The quotient version C(r,k)=rC(r−1,k)/(r−k) requires r≠k.

At r=k, both sides of the division-free equation are zero, but dividing by r−k would be invalid. A correct identity can have a misleading solved form.

For integers 0≤k≤m≤n, choosing an m-subset and then a k-subset inside it gives C(n,m)C(m,k). Choose the k-subset first instead, then add m−k members from the remaining n−k objects. This gives C(n,k)C(n−k,m−k). It is the same nested pair of subsets counted in two orders.

Factorial cancellation verifies the algebra in the integer domain. For polynomial extensions, fix lower indices and prove an identity as a polynomial in the upper variable; equality at infinitely many nonnegative integers then proves the polynomial identity. Numerical agreement at a few points alone is not that proof.

passages.title: Write the side condition beside the rewrite
passages.text:
A useful transformation records which variables are integers, which denominators must be nonzero, and whether out-of-range coefficients use the zero convention. Avoid applying factorial formulas with a negative-integer factorial or extending symmetry to a noninteger lower index.

For a fixed lower k, C(r,k) is a polynomial of degree k, so identities can survive at values where an intermediate quotient fails. Resolve this by using the polynomial identity itself, not by assigning a value to 0/0. The ability to manipulate symbols depends on maintaining these domains.

passages.title: Every final set determines its own split
passages.text:
Take disjoint groups A and B of sizes r and s. To choose n objects from their union, let k be the number chosen from A. For this fixed k there are C(r,k)C(s,n−k) possibilities. Different k values describe disjoint cases, and every chosen n-set has exactly one such k. Summing gives Vandermonde’s identity.

The scene uses r=3, s=4, n=3. The case totals are 4,18,12,1, which add to 35=C(7,3). A bin depicts a case count, not a single representative set multiplied accidentally by the same count again.

passages.title: Make the finite support explicit · More groups produce multinomial coefficients
passages.text:
For nonnegative integer r,s,n, only max(0,n−s)≤k≤min(r,n) can contribute. Using zero coefficients outside the counting range permits a simpler sum from k=0 to n. If n>r+s, both sides are zero. If n=0, the single empty choice contributes 1.

The proof depends on the two groups being disjoint. If one object belonged to both categories and could be chosen twice through different descriptions, the product count would need correction. Counting by a property works when the property assigns each outcome to exactly one case.

For disjoint groups, repeat the two-stage partition to obtain multiway convolutions. In a related assignment problem, place n distinct objects into labeled categories with prescribed sizes k₁,…,kₘ summing to n. The count is n!/(k₁!⋯kₘ!), obtained by choosing each category’s members from those remaining.

This coefficient also appears in (x₁+⋯+xₘ)ⁿ: each term records one category choice per factor. Category labels matter; forgetting them changes the equivalence relation and generally changes the count.

passages.title: Use polynomial coefficients for the generalized identity
passages.text:
The notation [zⁿ] means the coefficient multiplying the power zⁿ; for example, [z²](1+3z+7z²)=7. Multiply (1+z)ʳ and (1+z)ˢ and take the coefficient of zⁿ. For integer r,s this is ordinary polynomial multiplication. For real r,s, generalized binomial series converge absolutely when |z|<1, and the coefficient of fixed degree n uses only n+1 terms. The product is (1+z)ʳ⁺ˢ, so the same finite convolution identity holds for real upper indices and nonnegative integer n.

This is a separate algebraic/analytic justification. A half-object subset interpretation does not become valid merely because the formula extends.

passages.title: Differences uncover a better polynomial basis
passages.text:
The forward difference Δf(x)=f(x+1)−f(x) replaces neighboring values by their difference. For f(x)=x³ at x=0,1,2,3,4, the successive rows begin 0,1,8,27,64; then 1,7,19,37; then 6,12,18; then 6,6. A degree-three polynomial has a constant third difference.

Ordinary powers are natural for derivatives; falling factorials are natural for differences because Δx underlined k=k x underlined (k−1). Equivalently, ΔC(x,k)=C(x,k−1). Here Δᵏf(0) is the first entry after k rounds of taking adjacent differences, with Δ⁰f(0)=f(0); d denotes the degree of the polynomial. The difference table therefore gives the Newton expansion f(x)=Σₖ Δᵏf(0)C(x,k) for any polynomial f.

passages.title: Partition fibers to convert ordinary powers · Use the new basis to sum a polynomial
passages.text:
Let S(n,k) count partitions of an n-element labeled set into k nonempty unlabeled blocks. Count functions from that set into x labeled targets, first for nonnegative integer x. There are xⁿ functions. Alternatively, partition the domain into its k nonempty fibers, then assign distinct target labels to those blocks in x underlined k ways. Thus xⁿ=Σₖ S(n,k)x underlined k. Since both sides are polynomials, the identity extends to every real or complex x.

The bases are S(0,0)=1, S(n,0)=0 for n>0, and zero outside 0≤k≤n. Adding a new element either puts it in one of k existing blocks or makes a new singleton, proving S(n+1,k)=kS(n,k)+S(n,k−1).

For cubes, the second-kind coefficients are S(3,1)=1, S(3,2)=3, S(3,3)=1. Thus x³=x underlined 1+3x underlined 2+x underlined 3. Sum from x=0 through N−1 and apply the falling-factorial antidifference term by term. This yields N underlined 2/2 + N underlined 3 + N underlined 4/4, equal to [N(N−1)/2]².

The implementation checks small set partitions exhaustively and verifies polynomial identities coefficient by coefficient. A table of evaluated points is useful testing, but the fiber argument and induction establish the identities in general.

passages.title: First-kind coefficients undo the change of basis
passages.text:
Let c(n,k) be the unsigned Stirling number of the first kind, counting permutations of n labels with k cycles. Insert the newest label after one of the n existing labels in a cycle, or make it a singleton cycle. This proves c(n+1,k)=n c(n,k)+c(n,k−1), with c(0,0)=1 and the same zero conventions.

The signed coefficient s(n,k)=(−1)ⁿ⁻ᵏc(n,k) expands the falling factorial: x underlined n=Σₖs(n,k)xᵏ. Induction follows by multiplying by x−n. These signed first-kind and second-kind triangular coefficient arrays are inverse changes of basis; the unsigned array alone does not supply the inverse signs.

passages.title: Small positive increments can still escape every bound
passages.text:
Define H₀=0 and Hₙ=Σₖ₌₁ⁿ1/k for integer n≥1. Every new bar has smaller height, so the growth slows. But in the group 2ʲ<k≤2ʲ⁺¹ there are 2ʲ terms, each at least 1/2ʲ⁺¹. Every such group contributes at least 1/2. After m groups, H₂ᵐ≥1+m/2.

As m can be arbitrarily large, the harmonic sequence is unbounded. This is a proof of divergence; an upward-looking finite chart would not be one. Shrinking terms alone do not imply a finite sum.

passages.title: A decreasing curve brackets the rectangles
passages.text:
The function 1/x is positive and decreasing on x>0. On [k,k+1], its integral is at most 1/k. Summing gives ln(n+1)≤Hₙ. On [k−1,k] for k≥2, its integral is at least 1/k, giving Hₙ≤1+ln n. These inequalities hold for n≥1 and use the natural logarithm.

The lower curve area and upper rectangle sum are different objects. The picture helps identify which lies above which, while the monotonicity argument supplies the bound for every interval.

passages.title: A limiting offset refines the logarithmic scale · Use bounds as a scale estimate
passages.text:
The sequence Hₙ−ln n decreases and stays positive. Indeed, its change is 1/(n+1)−ln(1+1/n)<0 because the integral of 1/x on [n,n+1] exceeds its right-endpoint rectangle. The lower integral bound keeps Hₙ−ln n above zero. Hence it has a limit, called Euler’s constant γ.

This establishes the existence of γ without computing its decimal digits. The stronger expansion Hₙ=ln n+γ+1/(2n)−1/(12n²)+⋯ requires an error-controlled asymptotic theorem and is deferred to later material. A rounded estimate of the offset is not its exact definition.

To roughly double a large harmonic total, n must grow far more than by a factor of two; the leading growth is logarithmic. Doubling n adds a quantity approaching ln 2, not another copy of Hₙ. The exact rational model and logarithmic bounds are different kinds of information and are labeled accordingly.

At n=0 the definition H₀=0 still works, but the bounds involving ln n do not. Every use of the logarithm must retain n≥1. Later algorithm costs often contain harmonic sums because a success probability or contribution at stage k is proportional to 1/k.

passages.title: The same reciprocal appears in many rows
passages.text:
Write H₁,H₂,…,Hₙ as rows of a triangular grid. Row i contains 1,1/2,…,1/i. The column for reciprocal 1/j begins at row j and ends at row n, so it contains n−j+1 copies. Count by columns instead of rows to evaluate Σᵢ₌₁ⁿHᵢ.

The total is Σⱼ₌₁ⁿ(n−j+1)/j=(n+1)Hₙ−n. Every tile retains its pair (i,j) when the grouping changes. This is a finite reindexing identity, so convergence of an infinite series is irrelevant.

passages.title: A second identity separates diagonal and off-diagonal terms · Choose a rearrangement that simplifies multiplicity
passages.text:
Expand Hₙ²=ΣᵢΣⱼ1/(ij). The strict lower and strict upper triangles have equal totals after swapping i and j. The diagonal contributes Hₙ⁽²⁾=Σₖ1/k². The sum Σₖ Hₖ/k is the lower triangle including the diagonal. It therefore equals half the square total plus half the diagonal total.

This proof explains the plus sign: the diagonal is included once in the desired triangle but only half a time in half of the square. Add the missing half.

When a harmonic number appears inside another finite sum, expand its definition and inspect how often each reciprocal occurs. A weight depending on the row may require summing those weights across the column. Summation by parts is another route when the differences of the weight simplify.

For n=0 both displayed finite identities give zero. Rational arithmetic keeps all finite examples exact; the model does not equate a finite Hₙ⁽²⁾ with ζ(2). A limit value and a partial sum differ by the positive tail, even when their rounded displays happen to agree.

passages.title: Higher reciprocal powers have a convergence threshold
passages.text:
For real r, define the finite generalized harmonic sum Hₙ⁽ʳ⁾=Σₖ₌₁ⁿk⁻ʳ. If r>1, the infinite sum converges to ζ(r). The integral comparison bounds the tail after n≥1 between (n+1)¹⁻ʳ/(r−1) and n¹⁻ʳ/(r−1). These bounds tend to zero.

If r≤1, then k⁻ʳ≥1/k for k≥1, so the series diverges by comparison with the harmonic series. The symbol ζ(r) has an advanced analytic continuation elsewhere, but that continuation is not the value of this divergent positive-term series.

passages.title: A local two-slot update carries the entire sequence
passages.text:
Define F₀=0, F₁=1, and Fₙ₊₂=Fₙ₊₁+Fₙ for every n≥0. The vector (Fₙ₊₁,Fₙ) updates by the matrix Q with rows (1,1) and (1,0). Multiplication replaces the first slot by the sum and the second by the old first slot.

A separate counting interpretation uses a length-m walkway tiled by pieces of length 1 or 2. Its count Tₘ satisfies T₀=T₁=1 and Tₘ=Tₘ₋₁+Tₘ₋₂ by examining the first tile. Thus Tₘ=Fₘ₊₁; the index shift is essential.

passages.title: Multiply transformations to obtain an addition law · A determinant explains the alternating sign
passages.text:
Induction on n≥1 gives Qⁿ with entries Fₙ₊₁,Fₙ in its first row and Fₙ,Fₙ₋₁ in its second. The base n=1 is Q itself. Multiplication by Q adds neighboring Fibonacci entries and proves the next case.

Use Qᵐ⁺ⁿ=QᵐQⁿ. Comparing an off-diagonal entry yields Fₘ₊ₙ=FₘFₙ₊₁+Fₘ₋₁Fₙ for m≥1,n≥0. It is a theorem for arbitrary indices, not a pattern guessed from a few values. The n=0 case reduces to Fₘ=Fₘ·1+Fₘ₋₁·0.

The determinant of Q is −1. Determinants multiply, so det(Qⁿ)=(−1)ⁿ. Substituting its Fibonacci entries gives Cassini’s identity Fₙ₊₁Fₙ₋₁−Fₙ²=(−1)ⁿ for n≥1. The two diagonal products in the scene differ by precisely one, with a sign that alternates at each matrix step.

At n=1 this reads 1·0−1²=−1. The formula as written uses Fₙ₋₁, so n=0 is excluded unless negative-index Fibonacci numbers are introduced. Q⁰ is the identity matrix and needs no negative-index convention.

The accompanying small walkway enumerates the recurrence combinatorially: remove its first single plank or its first double plank. The remaining lengths are m−1 and m−2, so the two disjoint classes sum to T_m=F_(m+1). This is a concrete witness of the same local recurrence used in the matrix proof.

passages.title: Extract consequences without erasing their hypotheses
passages.text:
Any common divisor of Fₙ and Fₙ₊₁ divides the left side of Cassini’s identity and hence divides 1. Thus consecutive Fibonacci numbers are coprime. The determinant argument does not claim that every pair is coprime; F₆=8 and F₉=34 have gcd 2.

A tiling proof of an addition identity must distinguish whether a double tile crosses the chosen seam. Ignoring the crossing case loses arrangements. The matrix proof packages both possibilities in the two terms of the product.

passages.title: Run Euclid on the indices, track a different invariant
passages.text:
For nonnegative m,n, not both zero, the Fibonacci gcd theorem states gcd(Fₘ,Fₙ)=F_gcd(m,n). The display runs Euclid on (m,n); beneath each index it computes the corresponding Fibonacci value. The index remainders are not claimed to be the remainders of the values.

With indices 15 and 9, the index chain is (15,9),(9,6),(6,3),(3,0). The value pairs are (610,34),(34,8),(8,2),(2,0). Every pair has value gcd 2, although 610 mod 34=32 is not F₆=8.

passages.title: Use the addition identity to preserve common divisors · Finish at zero and recover the theorem
passages.text:
For m≥1 and n≥0, Fₘ₊ₙ=FₘFₙ₊₁+Fₘ₋₁Fₙ. For n≥1, Fₙ is positive, and modulo Fₙ this is Fₘ₊ₙ≡FₘFₙ₊₁. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers Fₙ,Fₙ₊₁ are coprime, so multiplying by Fₙ₊₁ does not change the gcd with Fₙ. Hence gcd(Fₘ₊ₙ,Fₙ)=gcd(Fₘ,Fₙ).

Repeatedly subtract n from the larger index m to obtain gcd(Fₘ,Fₙ)=gcd(Fₘ mod ₙ,Fₙ), where the subscript denotes the Fibonacci number at the index remainder. To avoid ambiguous typography, read this as “F at (m modulo n).”

Euclid’s algorithm on nonnegative indices reaches (d,0), where d=gcd(m,n). The preserved value gcd is then gcd(F_d,F₀)=gcd(F_d,0)=F_d, proving the result. When one initial index is zero, the same endpoint argument applies immediately. If both are zero, one may extend the theorem by defining gcd(0,0)=0; our main claim excludes that pair to avoid a convention dispute.

As a consequence, if a positive integer d divides n, then F_d divides Fₙ. The converse needs care at the repeated small values F₁=F₂=1; divisibility of values does not always identify divisibility of indices.

passages.title: Distinguish an invariant from an equality of remainders
passages.text:
Preserving a gcd is weaker than preserving an individual number or a numerical remainder. The counterexample in the opening trace is intentional: F₁₅ mod F₉=32, while F_(15 mod 9)=F₆=8. Both 32 and 8 have gcd 2 with F₉=34, which is exactly what the proof needs.

Integer arithmetic is used throughout; no rounded Binet values enter the gcd. A single off-by-one or floating error could change divisibility completely. The independent tests compare the theorem with ordinary integer gcd for many index pairs.

passages.title: Package a recurrence as coefficients
passages.text:
Let G(z)=Σₙ≥₀Fₙzⁿ. Treat this first as a formal power series: it is a sequence of coefficients, and multiplication is defined coefficient by coefficient. Subtract zG and z²G from G. Every coefficient of degree at least 2 vanishes by the recurrence, the constant term is zero, and the coefficient of z is one. Therefore (1−z−z²)G=z.

Since the denominator has nonzero constant coefficient, it has a unique formal-series inverse. No analytic convergence claim is needed for this algebraic derivation. As an analytic series, G converges for |z|<1/φ, where φ=(1+√5)/2 is the positive root of r²=r+1.

passages.title: Split the denominator into two geometric streams · A small exact error makes nearest-integer recovery possible
passages.text:
Let φ=(1+√5)/2 and ψ=(1−√5)/2. They satisfy φ+ψ=1, φψ=−1, and each root obeys r²=r+1. Factoring the denominator and using partial fractions gives G(z)=(1/√5)(1/(1−φz)−1/(1−ψz)). Taking the coefficient of zⁿ gives Binet’s formula.

Independently verify it: at n=0 the numerator is zero; at n=1 it is √5; and both root powers satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence. A second-order recurrence with those two initial values has a unique sequence, so the formula holds for every n≥0.

Because |ψ|<1, the exact real number φⁿ/√5 differs from Fₙ by |ψ|ⁿ/√5≤1/√5<1/2 for n≥0. Thus Fₙ is the nearest integer to φⁿ/√5. The scene draws the leading term near the exact integer and shows the correction from the second root; the drawn coordinates use rounded floats, while the integer label comes from the recurrence.

The error bound concerns exact real arithmetic. It does not bound the numerical error introduced by storing φ and repeatedly raising an approximation to powers.

passages.title: Floating computation can invalidate the rounding shortcut
passages.text:
A floating approximation to φ has a small relative error, but exponentiation magnifies it. Eventually the resulting absolute error exceeds half a unit, and rounding produces the wrong integer. The model’s separate precision check compares the ordinary double-precision expression with exact Fibonacci recurrence values and records an actual mismatch; it does not hide the failure behind the theorem.

For reliable large integers, use the integer recurrence or a tested fast-doubling method. If using high-precision real arithmetic, carry a certified numerical error bound in addition to the exact ψ correction. Algebraic exactness and machine accuracy are different obligations.
